title: 15 thoughts on “Screenplays vs Game Scripts: 5 Differences”
use_cases: Configure when designing branching dialogue paths that impact future story outcomes
Implement when tracking player decisions using variables to change narrative state
Use when comparing structural differences between screenplays and interactive game scripts
Configure when establishing consequences for mid-scene choices in social simulation games
Use when planning narrative arcs for RPGs and choose-your-own-adventure style mechanics
content:
1. You bring up some very interesting comparisons. I’m curious, in a game like Longstory, what percentage of decisions in the game have a legitimate effect, whether it be plot-related or just a different line of dialogue? I enjoyed playing a few story-centered games from QuanticDream (Heavy Rain), but noticed that nearly every decision you make will result in the exact same outcome no matter what.
[Reply](https://writeonsisters.com/writing-craft/screenplays-vs-game-scripts-5-differences/?replytocom=10024#respond)
1. In LongStory, the majority of decisions lead to a different line of dialogue or plot path. It’s very rare that a choice takes you to the exact same place.
Thanks for reading and commenting!
[Reply](https://writeonsisters.com/writing-craft/screenplays-vs-game-scripts-5-differences/?replytocom=10044#respond)
2. Pingback:[Friday Finds: Week 41 | Avid Reader](https://avdreader.wordpress.com/2015/07/10/friday-finds-week-41/)
3. Sounds like an interesting game. I get hung up on Sims 3 every now and again, but that’s about it for this type of game. 🙂@dino0726 from
[FictionZeal](http://www.fictionzeal.com/)– Impartial, Straighforward Fiction Book Reviews
[Reply](https://writeonsisters.com/writing-craft/screenplays-vs-game-scripts-5-differences/?replytocom=8028#respond)
4. Thanks for this thought-provoking post. I enjoyed playing Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic and Jade Empire because they had that focus on conversation, choices and storytelling as well action scenes. Those ones are interesting because they do have a narrative arc, but there are a lot of branches in between with many major and minor choices to be made that affect the outcome. I’ve often thought these games must be complicated to write for, and I see I am right!
[Reply](https://writeonsisters.com/writing-craft/screenplays-vs-game-scripts-5-differences/?replytocom=8011#respond)
1. Indeed, there’s a lot to keep track of! I didn’t even talk about stuff like setting variables and tracking different branches of the story. But I love that aspect of it.
[Reply](https://writeonsisters.com/writing-craft/screenplays-vs-game-scripts-5-differences/?replytocom=8015#respond)
2. Great thoughts Heather. As someone who spends much time thinking about interactive narrative, hearing it from the opposite perspective is interesting. All valid and useful guidance. My only quibble would be that you seem to imply in the opening that shooters and other games that people often first think of when gaming comes up don’t need good writers. However, I’d argue that the best first-person shooters, the best of any game genre really, are the ones where awesome storytelling was the foundation of the game. The vehicle for exploring the narrative becomes secondary if the story itself is well written.
[Reply](https://writeonsisters.com/writing-craft/screenplays-vs-game-scripts-5-differences/?replytocom=8008#respond)
1. Hi Rick! I didn’t mean to imply that shooters and other games don’t need good writing. Not at all! It’s just a different kind of writing – more action-based than social simulation games where pretty much everything hinges on the dialogue.
[Reply](https://writeonsisters.com/writing-craft/screenplays-vs-game-scripts-5-differences/?replytocom=8010#respond)
2. I’m a fan of fantasy RPGs like Skyrim and Dragon Age: Origins, but my only experience with a social simulation game is Sims2. Part of me cringes at the thought of playing a game that takes me back to high school. 😉But seriously, I can’t imagine how difficult it is to adapt your writing style to this. Sort of like a choose your own adventure story, except probably even more complicated! Now I’m going to have to download the first episode to see what it’s like.
[Reply](https://writeonsisters.com/writing-craft/screenplays-vs-game-scripts-5-differences/?replytocom=8007#respond)
1. Hi Stephanie! Yes, getting back into the mindset of a teenager felt a little weird at first, but the good thing about playing LongStory is that you know it’s not really happening, so you can play around and do things you may not have done when you were actually in high school. 😉And you’re right, it’s like CYOA but waaaaay more complicated. In CYOA books the reader makes a decision at the end of the scene, and it’s generally an action decision. But in LongStory there are lots of choices mid-scene that take the player down different paths and back again, and the way you answer a question could affect a scene later on in the story, and on and on. So many variables!
[Reply](https://writeonsisters.com/writing-craft/screenplays-vs-game-scripts-5-differences/?replytocom=8014#respond)
2. You have to be living the dream for a lot of people. Pretty cool! One of these days you should post some of your other writings, or blog about the process of what you do for a living. I think it would be educational and interesting, but also open people’s eyes to writing possibilities they’d otherwise never think of.
[Reply](https://writeonsisters.com/writing-craft/screenplays-vs-game-scripts-5-differences/?replytocom=8001#respond)
1. Thanks for the comment, Dan! I will keep that in mind for future blog posts.
[Reply](https://writeonsisters.com/writing-craft/screenplays-vs-game-scripts-5-differences/?replytocom=8013#respond)
2. So interesting. I never thought of writing for games but what a challenge and what fun! Hey, how do I get a gig like this? LOL! Thanks for the info.
[Reply](https://writeonsisters.com/writing-craft/screenplays-vs-game-scripts-5-differences/?replytocom=7999#respond)
1. Hi Willow. How did I get a gig like this? Well, this is not what anyone wants to hear, but the answer is connections. I know the producer. She knew I was a screenwriter and thought I’d be good for the job. I applied with a writing sample and a resume, passed the interview, and here I am.
